playful: A piece that hasn't been through Editorial yet — and if it's leaving the building in this state, it had better be stamped Draft or Unedited so nobody mistakes it for final.
real: A document that has not yet been submitted to Editorial for review; recommended practice is to clearly label such documents as Draft or Unedited before external distribution.

playful: Feedback from the client that arrives early, off the official record — Account's job is to double-check it matches the official version once that finally comes through the system.
real: Medical-legal review comments provided directly by the client before being formally released through the official submission system; Account is responsible for reconciling these against the official comments once received.

playful: How it actually feels to use something — a website, an app, or (fittingly) a dictionary like this one.
real: The overall experience of an end-user interacting with a product, service, or system.

playful: The little starburst or banner slapped across an ad shouting 'NEW INDICATION!' or 'NOW ONCE-DAILY!' — deliberately breaking the clean design to grab your eye first.
real: An intrusive visual element, such as a banner or starburst, that disrupts a design's original layout, typically used to announce new information.

playful: A sales rep's actual pitch tool — meant to be shown to a doctor during a conversation, not handed over to be read alone. Goes by several names: visAid, iVis on an iPad, or detail aid.
real: A printed or digital piece designed to support a sales representative's presentation of information to healthcare providers, intended to be shown during a conversation rather than read independently. Also called a visAid, iVis, or detail aid.

playful: The IRS form every freelancer and vendor fills out at least once — confirms your tax ID before anyone gets paid.
real: An IRS form providing a U.S. taxpayer's identification number, used by businesses to collect vendor or freelancer tax information before payment.

playful: Three letters that quietly reshaped the entire agency world.
real: Shorthand for working remotely rather than in an office.

playful: The recurring check-in where a team and Shared Services compare notes on where every project actually stands.
real: A weekly meeting where teams gather with shared services to discuss project status and updates.

playful: A single short line stranded at the top of a page, cut off from the rest of its paragraph — editors reword or respace text specifically to avoid leaving one behind.
real: A short line ending a paragraph that gets separated from the rest of the paragraph by a column or page break; typically avoided through wording or spacing adjustments.

playful: The budget for a script's spoken words, set before production even starts — go over, and suddenly the video's too long for its own timeline and postproduction budget.
real: The number of words spoken in a script, estimated at the start of an interactive project to keep the script within the scope of its planned duration and budget.

playful: Two very different intensities of proofing. A Slug check is the fast version — just confirm the first and last word of each line match the backup. A Word-for-Word Read is the exhaustive version — every single word, graphic, and label checked against backup, nothing skipped.
real: A Slug check verifies only the first and last word of each line against the previous approved version, confirming line breaks haven't shifted. A Word-for-Word Read is a full comparison of every word, graphic, and label against backup, the most rigorous level of proofing.

playful: The project-management platform many agencies route work through, plus the formal request tickets — generated by Project Management, emailed to the right department — that tell a team exactly what needs to get built or changed.
real: Workfront is a widely used project-management platform for routing and tracking creative and production work. A Workfront request is a formal ticket generated by Project Management, containing the information a specific department needs to execute a task.

playful: The height of a lowercase letter measured without any of the tall or dangly bits — basically, how big the letter 'x' looks in a given font.
real: The height of a lowercase letter excluding its ascender or descender, a key measurement in typography.

playful: The 'full disclosure' ad — it names the drug, names what it treats, and by law has to give the risks just as much airtime as the benefits.
real: An official FDA advertising category. A Product Claim Ad names both the drug and the condition it treats, and is legally required to present fair-balanced risk and benefit information.

playful: The ad that just says the drug's name and basically nothing else — a billboard that exists purely to keep the brand top-of-mind.
real: An official FDA advertising category. A Reminder Ad names the drug but does not state what condition it treats, which historically exempted it from including full risk information.

playful: The ad that never mentions a drug at all — just 'do you have these symptoms? Talk to your doctor,' quietly setting the stage for a launch still to come.
real: An official FDA advertising category, also called Disease Awareness Communication. It discusses a condition and encourages viewers to see a doctor, without naming any specific drug — often used ahead of a product launch.

term: Ask Your Doctor If [Drug] Is Right For You
playful: The universal closing line of every DTC ad ever made. Never 'take this drug' — always 'ask if it's right for you,' because the actual prescribing decision legally has to happen between you and an HCP, not a 30-second spot.
real: A standard direct-to-consumer advertising phrase reflecting that a licensed prescriber, not the advertisement, must make the actual treatment decision.

playful: The visual shorthand of DTC advertising: an attractive couple, usually 55-plus, walking or running along a beach, implying that whatever ailment they had is now thoroughly behind them.
real: A recurring aspirational-lifestyle visual convention in pharmaceutical advertising — showing vitality and independence — used because lifestyle imagery isn't restricted the way specific efficacy claims are.

playful: The fast, flat voiceover listing every possible side effect while the visuals keep smiling and gardening like nothing was just said.
real: The spoken risk disclosure required in broadcast DTC ads — delivered quickly to fit runtime, while imagery continues, a format frequently criticized by researchers for reducing how well viewers actually retain the risk information.

playful: The warm, sun-drenched lighting every DTC ad seems to film in — nothing says 'hope' quite like backlighting.
real: A cinematographic convention using warm, low-angle lighting (typical of the hour after sunrise or before sunset) to convey optimism and emotional warmth in advertising.

playful: The extreme close-up of hands demonstrating exactly how to click, twist, or press a drug's delivery device — because if you're about to self-inject something, the ad wants zero room for confusion.
real: A common visual sequence in biologic and insulin advertising, showing step-by-step device operation to support patient self-administration.

playful: The four words doing the most legal heavy lifting in the entire ad, usually in the smallest font on screen.
real: A standard disclaimer indicating that individual outcomes shown in testimonials or demonstrations may not be typical or guaranteed.

playful: The tiny on-screen text that answers the question you didn't know you were supposed to ask: is this heartwarming testimonial real, or is it SAG-AFTRA?
real: A required disclosure distinguishing genuine patient testimonials from paid actors portraying a patient experience in advertising.

playful: The last few seconds of the ad, quietly mentioning that eligible patients might pay as little as [suspiciously specific dollar amount] per month — the savings-card pitch tacked onto the emotional close.
real: An advertising segment promoting a manufacturer copay assistance or savings card program, aimed at offsetting patient out-of-pocket costs.

playful: The oddly specific cartoon character invented to represent a side effect or disease state — giving something uncomfortable a friendlier, more marketable face.
real: A recurring DTC advertising technique using an original character or visual metaphor to represent a medical condition or side effect in an approachable, memorable way.

playful: The on-screen text making sure nobody mistakes a drug commercial for genuine breaking news, no matter how it's styled.
real: A required on-screen disclosure identifying certain advertising formats (particularly those styled like editorial or news content) as paid promotional material.

playful: The wall of text scrolling up the screen in a digital or print ad, technically readable, functionally a speed-reading test.
real: On-screen scrolling or static risk-information text used to satisfy fair-balance requirements in digital and print advertising formats.

playful: The 'coming soon, no spoilers' stage of a drug launch — ads raise awareness of a condition for months before the actual drug name ever shows up.
real: A pre-launch marketing phase using Help-Seeking / Disease Awareness advertising to build condition awareness ahead of a branded campaign, without naming the product.

playful: Grandparents playing catch, a couple laughing over dinner, someone finally gardening again — all in gentle slow motion, all implying one thing: life got its color back.
real: A recurring emotional-payoff visual convention in DTC advertising, using slow-motion lifestyle footage to signal restored quality of life as the ultimate benefit of treatment.
